description: Olá, sou estudante do 6º semestre de Ciência da Computação e estou liderando o projeto ARES — Marswalk Planning (no desafio Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map). Tenho conhecimentos em Python, análise e visualização de dados, design de interfaces (UI) e prototipagem rápida apoiada por IA. Meu foco é transformar dados complexos de exploração espacial em uma ferramenta tática, limpa e intuitiva para apoiar a segurança e a tomada de decisão de astronautas em superfície marciana.
summary:
ARES — Marswalk Planning is a tactical EVA (extravehicular activity) navigation and decision-support dashboard designed to help astronauts safely plan and execute surface routes on Mars. Focusing on Jezero Crater (Mission to Rochette), ARES unifies dispersed NASA planetary data layers—optical, slope, thermal (Night IR), and regional relief—into a single mission-control interface. By enforcing terrain safety policies (automatically detecting steep slopes >15° and environmental hazards), ARES blocks high-risk paths and recommends safe, terrain-aware detours, drastically reducing astronaut cognitive load under extreme operational pressure.

PT-BR
O ARES — Marswalk Planning é um painel tático de navegação e suporte à decisão desenvolvido para ajudar astronautas a planejar e executar caminhadas seguras (marswalks) na superfície de Marte. Focado na região da Cratera Jezero (Missão para Rochette), o ARES unifica camadas dispersas de dados planetários da NASA — imagens ópticas, análise de declividade (slope), infravermelho noturno (Night IR) e relevo regional — em uma única interface estilo sala de controle. Ao validar regras rigorosas de segurança do terreno (bloqueando automaticamente rotas que cruzam encostas íngremes acima de 15° e sugerindo desvios seguros), o sistema reduz a carga cognitiva do explorador sob alta pressão, garantindo a integridade da tripulação durante missões científicas.
details:
How It Works ARES — Marswalk Planning is a web-based tactical navigation and decision-support dashboard designed for astronauts and mission controllers operating on the Martian surface, focused on Jezero Crater (Mission to Rochette). Instead of forcing explorers to cross-reference dispersed scientific files under high-pressure field conditions, ARES consolidates multi-layer planetary datasets—Optical imagery, Slope analysis, Night IR (thermal), and Regional Relief—into a single dark-mode mission-control interface. Users can inspect terrain layers, compare candidate routes (such as direct paths versus terrain-aware detours), view round-trip distance, marching time, and safety reserves, and receive automated "ROUTE BLOCKED" warnings whenever a path violates terrain slope policies (greater than 15°).

Benefits & Intended Impact ARES translates complex orbital and surface telemetry into immediate, actionable "go or reroute" visual verdicts, drastically reducing cognitive load during extravehicular activities. Prioritizing crew survival first, the system enforces spacesuit mobility and terrain safety thresholds before an astronaut enters hazardous slopes or thermal anomalies. By balancing scientific exploration goals with safe return margins, ARES bridges the gap between planetary science data and real-time human field execution.

Tools, Languages & Resources Used The platform was built using Python, Streamlit, HTML/CSS, and interactive geospatial mapping libraries with layered terrain controls. The mission data and interface design were inspired by NASA/JPL Mars Trek, USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping datasets, and Jezero Crater mission telemetry. In accordance with hackathon guidelines, generative AI tools were used strictly as a technical copilot to accelerate UI prototyping, code structuring, documentation formatting, and the creation of the minimalist team emblem.

Creative Aspect & Key Factors Considered The creative aspect lies in applying a high-contrast, low-glare mission-control and spacesuit HUD design philosophy combined with binary terrain-policy enforcement, allowing an explorer to read critical hazards in seconds. Key engineering and operational factors considered include heavy spacesuit torque and balance limits on steep inclines (greater than 15°), visibility constraints, round-trip time and safety reserve margins, and seamless cross-layer terrain verification across optical, thermal, and relief datasets.
